title: Shop Hands
passages:
The tender came onto Anza's ore stub at walking pace and stopped all at once, the way it always did, brakes letting go a long sigh that turned to fog under the lamps. Rhea was down on the deck plate before the wheels quit turning. Her reader sat in her coat pocket with a spent cartridge in it, dead since the Weir, and dead was no use to her, because the thing she needed read was two hundred meters off in the relay shop where her brother was breathing off a shop bottle.

"Nothing on this stub bites," Coombs said, coming down behind her with the slate held flat.

"Everything on this stub bites. You haven't been introduced."

The blank-plated rig was already there. No number on the plate, no transponder, brakes set hard, and canisters still decked in two strapped rows with frost furred along the webbing. Steam came off the deck in slow ropes. That meant the load was warm, and a warm load meant it had been sealed and stacked somewhere with heat in it, and the nearest somewheres were all north.

Doan stood at the rig's step with a hand lamp on them and a loop of orange locker cord around one wrist, the other end going up into the overlap locker housing. Assisted inspection, which at Anza meant somebody stood close enough to see your hands.

Coombs turned the slate face-up and held it out. Two fields, both blank, both waiting.

"Name," he said, pleasant as a man selling water in a dry month. "Give me a name and a logged wage, and a bunk with a lamp that stays on, and nobody reads your file twice."

Doan looked at the slate the way you look at a dog you've already kicked.

"No."

"Then walk for me. Ten steps, that's all it takes."

"No."

"He's got you, puller," Miko said, dropping off the deck with her collar up. "That's a no on both fields. Try the woman with the tape on her hand, she's cheaper."

"I'm not on your slate," Doan said. "Names are what froze this node. You want one, take it off the board. There's a bay number where a name goes."

Bale came down last, tube capped under his arm, and did not look at any of them. "Officer Bale, Kettering desk remand. I don't need the slate. I need a confirm or a no before the bell, and then I carry it up to the morning desk myself."

"When's the bell," Rhea said.

"Nine minutes."

"Then I need a cartridge." She was already moving toward the locker housing, toward the cord. "Reader spares live in the overlap locker. Yours. With a dead key in it."

"Then you need a key that works," Doan said.

Wren had not come off the deck. She stood at the rail with her splinted hand held against her chest, looking at the canisters, and her lips were going.

"Eleven," she said.

"Stop that," Coombs said.

"Eleven," Wren said again, to nobody, the way you'd read a gauge.

Rhea got her bar out and set it under the locker housing's lip, and that was when the blank rig's brakes let go half a notch on their own, a hard dry clack, and the whole deck shifted a hand's width toward the drop.

Doan's lamp came up. "That wasn't me. I'm tied to the locker, look at me, that wasn't me."

Coombs's slate was still face-up in his hands, still blank in both fields, and the canisters on the rig ticked as they cooled, and Wren kept counting under her breath like she was being paid for it.

Rhea left the bar standing in the locker lip and walked Wren the two hundred meters to the relay shop, because a fresh cartridge was no use to anybody if the drawer that held them was at the wrong end of the stub behind a dead key.

The shop smelled like hot dust and old coffee. Teodoro stood at the grille with his palm flat on it, listening to the mains the way another man would listen to a radio. Ivo was in the chair by the compressor with the shop bottle between his knees — a hundred-bar flask of breathing air, three days in it if the patch held — and Marlowe sat on the bench with a chipped cup he had no plans to drink from, shoulder splinted at an angle that said somebody had done it properly.

"Eleven," Wren said.

"Not in here." Rhea pulled the parts tin out with her boot, found a reader cell, and thumbed it into her hand reader. Same cell reader two took. The screen came up amber and honest. "In here we do one thing at a time."

Nour was at the shift board with her coat still buttoned.

The board was chalk. Not paint, not glass — a slate panel that took a stick and gave it back, because a painted board can't be corrected and a chalk board can be corrected before the desk reads it. Fourth line down, in the column where a name goes, somebody had written a bay number.

Nour looked at it a while. Then she took it out with the heel of her hand, slow, the way you'd work a splinter loose.

"Number in that column reads as cargo," she said. "Name reads as crew. Name with a countersign in the same line reads as crew this node will feed, and I have eleven short canisters and a red chain, so I don't put my hand to what I can't feed." She held out the chalk stub. "Write it or get off my board."

"Chalk washes," Coombs said from the doorway. He had the slate under his arm, both fields still blank, which Rhea was starting to find worse than if he'd filled them. "Paper doesn't. There's a hold on her with the desk already."

"There's a hold on all of us," Nour said. "Sit down, puller."

Wren took the chalk in her left hand. Her right was splinted to a copper bar and taped flat, so the letters came out big and downhill, but they came out: WREN CARDOSO.

"Said counts," Teodoro said, without turning around. "Written alone it's a request."

Marlowe set the cup on the bench. He got the chalk out of her fingers, wrote his own name in the countersign slot under hers in small block letters, and said it out loud, flat, like a man reading a gauge he didn't like. "Marlowe. Living crew, shop hand, badge twenty-two forty-four."

The board took it. Chalk went gray into the slate and the shop's line printer chattered once by itself.

Teodoro lifted his palm off the grille. "That's two names in one line. Desk reads that as one address. When they send a tube for a household they send one tube and it takes what's at the address."

"Good," Marlowe said.

"You don't get to say good." Rhea's reader had gone from amber to green on Wren's walk, her voice, her bad left-handed letters, and Rhea believed it, because the machine had no reason to be kind. "Nine minutes ago you were cargo."

"Eight now," said Teodoro.

The bell went, flat and close, the way it did when the shift was changing and nobody had to be told twice.

Ivo pulled a breath off the bottle and made a face like a man who'd been sold water.

"This tastes like a glove," he said. "Wet one. Rubber and tape." He turned the flask to read the patch housing. "Whose hand did that come off? Because I'd like to know whose I'm breathing on."

Wren looked at the splint, then at him.

"Mine."

"Huh." Ivo took another breath and settled back. "Well. It holds."

Nour wiped the chalk dust off her palm onto her coat and looked up at the board, at two names in one line, and Rhea watched her do the arithmetic that everybody in the shop was refusing to do: chalk said crew, and the tube coming up the ore line said cargo, and there was no version of the desk that read both columns the same way.

PASSAGE-END

Miko came through the shop door with a rag bundle under her arm and the cold still on her collar.

"You're late," Kass said, without looking up. They had the board ledge for a desk: the palm-cut glove pinned flat to the cork with two seal nails, the tape across the knuckle gone gray, the hole in the palm clean as a punched washer. Nour's tally card sat face-out beside it, eleven seals short in a column, all down the same four runs.

"I'm on foot," Miko said. "You try it in this."

She set the bundle down and folded the rag back. Oilcloth, soft as a sock, corners rounded from being sat on. The overlap log — the book both shifts signed when one stayed past the bell and the next came early, so a canister that crossed in between carried a mark and nobody could say later it had never been counted.

"Yours," she said. "I've hauled it since Kettering and I'm tired of being the only one who knows what's in it."

"Bay Four to a tool void to an ore siding to a tender," Kass said. "Four hundred kilometers of courier work, unpaid."

"Then pay me in something that isn't paper."

Miko took the tickets out of her inside pocket, three of them, soft at the folds. She looked at them the way you look at a dog you might still buy. *Dalia Reyes. M. Ivers. Perrin Ault.* The last one had been written by somebody who didn't care whether it was a person or a cough.

"Green board at the Weir," she said. "Green means the coast trains are running. Running means a paid seat, and a seat means the coast, and the coast means winter somewhere with water in it." She put them back and buttoned the pocket. "It pulls in an hour and a half and I'd be sitting on it in a coat I'd freeze to death in. So no."

"So yes," Nour said, from the board.

"So put me on resupply." Miko tipped her head at the chalk. "Book shift, honest wage. I unload what comes down the line and I don't skim a canister, and if I do, you've got my name in your own handwriting to hold up at the desk."

"The book gets read," Nour said.

"Everything gets read. I'd rather be read holding a canister than holding nothing." She spread her hands. "Write me in under Miko. It's the only one of the four I've had long enough to owe money on."

Nour wrote her in. Fifth line down, own column, no countersign, because a resupply hand isn't crew, it's a pair of arms with a name attached.

Kass had not moved. They slid the tally card over until its edge touched the open page, then took the loupe out of the parts tin and set it to their eye.

Every entry on the page carried a crescent struck into the seal wax beside the bay line. Every crescent had a bite out of the lower horn on the left, about the size of a grain of rice. The tally card had the same crescent eleven times. Same bite. Same place. Same grain of rice.

Kass straightened up and did not say anything for long enough that Teodoro lifted his palm off the grille.

"Say it or put it down," Teodoro said.

"There was a die in the void with me," Miko said. "Kettering, Bay Four, riding on the deck plate by my boot the whole way down. Crescent, heavy, cold enough to stick to your hand. Chipped horn. Ospina found it when they opened the void and put it in their coat, and they still had it in the coat when they walked out of that desk this morning. Never stamped with it. I watched them not stamp with it."

"Where's Ospina now," Rhea said.

"Northbound. Posted rig, red ring." Kass set the loupe down on the ledge, very carefully, which from Kass was shouting. "Still holding it."

"Then it's a chip," Rhea said. "A chip is a chip. Half the dies on the Interior get dropped."

"Show me a second crescent with a rice grain out of the left horn and I'll buy you a drink at Culvert Nine." Kass turned the loupe a quarter turn with one finger so the light came through it. "This is the one. Same die, eleven times on that card, and every line of it on this page."

Nobody in the shop asked the next question, because everybody in the shop had already gotten there and none of them wanted to be the one who said it out loud in front of a chalk board.

"Pin it," Miko said. "Pin it and come unload something."

"Eleven," Wren said.

PASSAGE-END

Kass flattened the card on the housing lid and read it the way you read a gauge.

"Receiving mark, Anza stub, this jaw. Eleven canisters struck in full that came down the line short." They turned the log so the light fell across the page. "Same crescent, same chip. The jaw strikes what the receiving hand puts under it. So say the hand."

"I put them under it," Nour said.

"Louder. There's a puller standing here and a chalk board two hundred meters off."

"You want it in front of all of them." Nour's breath went out white and stayed. "I struck eleven short. Culvert Nine was owed a resupply stop and I paid it out of the down-line runs, and I struck them full so my board showed a fed node instead of a hole. That's the arrangement. That's why my roster's fat."

"And that's why I'm standing here," Doan said. "Cut it."

Nour didn't move. "No."

"His key's dead, his clearance is gone, and you've got him on assisted inspection with a hand lamp," Rhea said. "That's not a job, that's a fence post."

"The cord is the loop." Nour put her fist around the draw-line key in the housing, not lifting it, only holding it, the way you hold a rail on ice. "Locker stays live while a signed wrist closes the loop. Their wrist closes it. Live box issues seals, seals go down-line, down-line sends canisters back up, canisters feed my board through winter." She looked at Doan, and it wasn't unkind, which was worse. "Cut that and you're free and cold by Thursday and forty people on my chalk are cold with you."

"Then we'll be cold honest."

"You don't get to spend my node."

"I'm not spending it. I'm getting off it." Doan lifted the looped wrist an inch. The skin under the cord had gone the color of the cord. "Cut it, lid-hand. You've done it before."

Wren looked at the copper bar taped to her splint, then at the housing, where a seal knife hung on a lanyard with its edge turned inward, the way you keep a knife you use twice a shift.

"Knife's for seals," Nour said. "You cut a cord with it, the box logs a broken seal. That's the whole interlock. That's the rule."

"I know the rule." Wren took the knife in her left hand. "I counted them."

"Girl," Coombs said, "I've got a bunk with a lamp on it and a wage behind it, and you're about to price that man and forty others out of both."

"He asked twice," Wren said. "You only asked once."

She braced the cord against the housing lip, set the edge, and sawed. It took three passes. The copper bar knocked the box twice on the last one, and the orange cord parted, and the loose end went up over the pulley like something let out of a trap.

The bead in the bow of the key went out inside Nour's fist.

"Dead," Nour said. She held the key up where everyone could see it, cold brass, no light in it. "Twenty-two years I've kept that box live."

Rhea thumbed her reader. Amber, honest, useless. "One cell and no drawer."

Miko looked down the stub at the blank-plated rig with its two strapped rows and the steam still coming off the deck in slow ropes. "I just wrote my one honest name on a resupply shift," she said. "I'd like it noted that the line went dead inside of the minute."

"Noted," Kass said, and wrote it down, because Kass wrote down everything.

Doan shook the cut loop off their wrist and dropped it in the dust and stood there breathing like somebody who'd set down a canister they'd carried up a ladder. "So nothing stops here now," they said. "No seals, no jaw, no reason."

"Nothing stops here now," Nour said.

That was when Rhea heard it, down past the last stub lamp where the rails went into the dark and came out at the trestle. Not the dry clack the blank plate made when its brakes let go. This was underneath, in the rail itself, a low sound with a load behind it, and it came again, and again, evenly, patiently, at intervals too even to be weather. Her reader had nothing to say about it. She stood with her thumb on a dead cell and listened to the ore line and could not put a name to it.

Tick. Tick. Tick.

Rhea counted them before she decided to. Forty-foot rail on the ore line, a joint where each length butted the next, one flat tick per joint per wheel — so ticks arriving faster meant something was closing, and how fast was arithmetic she could do with a dead cell in her pocket.

"Nothing posts on this line at this hour," Kass said.

"Something's on it."

It came up past the last stub lamp with its lights burning. A number on the nose plate, 4409, and under the number a stripe of Kettering green, and a transponder mast with a live bulb on the top of it, which meant this rig answered when the master board asked where it was. Posted. Filed. Nobody had scrubbed it. It had come four hundred kilometers of dry ground on paperwork somebody had actually signed.

Three rigs on a stub built for two. Coombs's tender, the blank plate with its frost-furred rows, and now this, close enough that the posted rig's nose made one deck with the blank rig's tail.

The brakes took it with a hiss and a shudder, and it stopped, and nobody came off.

Then the crew box door cracked — the steel room behind the cab, where a rider sits when the rig drives itself — and V. Ospina came down the step with a file tube under one arm. Bay Four coveralls, hood down, face the color of the dust. Across the back of their right glove, a steel band with a bead set in the bow of it, blinking red. One blink a second, patient as a gauge.

"Which of you is Anza," Ospina said.

"All of us," Nour said. "That's the trouble with it."

"I've got a file." Ospina lifted the tube an inch. "Twenty-two forty-four. Physical recovery, opened at oh-eight-hundred, and there's a bell on it."

"Recovery of what," Rhea said.

"You know what."

"Say it," Doan said. "Everybody out here's had a name said over them tonight. It's your turn."

"Marlowe." Ospina said it without any weight at all, the way you read a line off a manifest. "Living crew on your plate. Cargo on my file. The desk wants the body inside the wire before the shift bell, and I'm the one they sent because my ring still seals."

Rhea looked at the red bead. "That thing's blinking."

"It's been blinking since the desk opened for review." Ospina turned the glove over so the light caught it. "Red doesn't stop it. Red means every seal it lays goes into the same review as mine — their name in my file, my clearance in their column, both of us standing at the desk explaining each other. So I don't lay it twice."

Miko put her collar up. "Comforting. A stamp that files you as a co-defendant."

"It files you as *known*," Ospina said. "There's worse."

Kass had not said anything. Kass was looking at Ospina's coat pocket, where something heavy hung and pulled the cloth down into a shape with a horn on it.

Bale came out of the lamplight with his tube capped under his arm, wax over the cap, his thumb resting on the wax the way another man would rest a thumb on a hammer.

"Officer Bale, Kettering desk remand." He held the tube up between them, not offering it. "I've got a confirm out of the Weir. It's got a name in it and the name isn't in your file."

"Mine's got a body in it."

"Then we've each got a sheet," Bale said, "and the desk reads one before the bell."

Ospina looked at him for a moment, then past him, down the stub at the dark where the rails went out toward the trestle, and then at Wren's splinted hand, at the copper bar taped flat across the palm.

"Four minutes," Ospina said. "Walk."

Rhea was already moving, because reader two was live in the shop and the man in the file was in the chair beside it with a cup he wasn't drinking. "Two hundred meters," she said. "Keep up, and don't touch my brother's bottle."

Behind them, the blank rig's brakes let go half a notch on their own — that dry clack, no hand on it — and the whole deck shifted a hand's width toward the drop.

Two hundred meters with a red ring counting at you is longer than two hundred meters.

Ospina walked like someone who had read the distance off a schedule. Rhea kept two fingers on Wren's elbow, because a splinted hand on lamp ice is how you lose the hand, and Miko came behind narrating.

"Three rigs on a two-rig stub," Miko said. "Somebody's going to write that up."

"Somebody always does," Doan said.

Coombs brought up the rear with the slate under their arm, both fields still blank, and Rhea had stopped finding that funny about a kilometer back.

The shop was hot after the stub, hot dust and old coffee, and Teodoro had his palm flat on the grille, listening to the mains. Reader two sat on the parts bench with its hood up: a plate of dark glass the size of a dinner tray, a hand-warm surface that takes a voice and a name and writes both into the living plate. A cold palm on it reads as weight. Weight is cargo. That was the whole difference between the columns on Nour's board and it takes two seconds to cross.

Ospina put the tube on the bench and unrolled the file — stiff gray desk stock, printed both sides, a blank at the foot the width of a thumb.

"Twenty-two forty-four," they said. "Physical recovery. It wants a living-crew statement, warm, in the man's own household, on this plate, countersigned by the ring that opened it." The bead blinked, one a second. "That's mine."

"It's blinking," Rhea said.

"It's blinked since oh-eight-hundred. Red doesn't stop a seal. Red means the seal and I go up in the same review." Ospina looked at Teodoro. "You'll go amber."

"Green is because Voss is listed as resealing authority," Teodoro said. "Amber is pending. Pending is a word that gets read out at a desk by somebody whose boots are wet."

"Then read fast," Ospina said.

Wren put her left hand on the glass. Reader two knew her already — it had her walk from the stub and her knuckles from the glove — so it only wanted the words.

"Name and count," Teodoro said.

Wren swore first, which Rhea took for a good sign.

"Wren Cardoso. Bay Four, lid-hand. He was warm." Her voice went down into the flat place where she kept the numbers. "All the way down, warm like a bunk. Swearing. Asked me twice if I knew what a shoulder was for, and then he asked me to stop, and I said three, and I said two." She breathed. "Lid down at twenty-one forty-four."

"Twenty-one forty-seven I was ballast," Marlowe said, from the bench. He set the chipped cup on the floor. "Three minutes is a long time to be wrong."

The plate wrote her name in the crew column, and under it a value field opened, wanting the last number.

"Two," Wren said.

Marlowe got up, crossed to the bench, and put his thumb on the glass beside her splint. "Not zero," he said. "I'm standing in it."

The plate took his print warm and wrote him under her, and the line printer chattered out a strip Rhea didn't reach for.

Ospina pressed the steel band flat to the glass. The bead stopped blinking and held, steady, the way a lamp holds when it's stopped pretending to be patient.

Teodoro's board chimed once. The chain light over the door went from green to amber, and stayed.

"Pending," Teodoro said.

"Known," Ospina said. "There's worse."

Bale came to the bench with his tube still capped, wax unbroken under his thumb. "That's my Weir confirm and your seal on one sheet," they said. "I carry it up myself, and I don't lose it in a coat."

"There's still a bunk with a lamp on it," Coombs said to Wren, from the doorway. "Warm. Logged. That offer's got a longer life than most."

"Not tonight," Wren said.

Ivo pulled a breath off the bottle and pointed at the amber light with the flask. "That thing cost us anything?"

"A shift," Teodoro said. "Maybe a node."

"Great. I've got three days of air and a glove in it." Ivo settled back. "Whose glove, again?"

"Mine," Wren said. "You're welcome."

Teodoro lifted his palm off the grille and stood very still, the way you do when the desk calls and you've been waiting on it since the shift before you.

The shop's line went from hiss to quiet.
